catalogTitle: דברים בטלים - חילוק העונש בין עם הארץ ותלמיד חכם. ביאור גודל חטא של ביטול תורה וביאור ענין חכמת חיצוניות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 8, the Mashgiach explains why bittul Torah and secular wisdom studied for its own sake are graver than idle talk, tracing secular wisdom to the fragments of the Breaking of the Vessels that remain within kelipas nogah.

abstract.en: Continuing Tanya chapter 8: forbidden speech belongs to the three impure kelipos and needs the 'hot laundry' of Gehinnom. An am ha'aretz who cannot learn and talks idle talk receives only a general punishment; today's irreligious Jews, who were never taught, are anusim and cannot be blamed. A talmid chacham who wastes his time, however, transgresses bittul Torah, which carries its own punishment. The Mashgiach contrasts Torah, learned lishmah, with secular wisdom, permitted only as a means, and explains why studying it for its own sake is worse than talk about baseball: it defiles the faculties of Chabad, not only the middos. Drawing on the Ramchal and the kings of Edom, he traces secular wisdom to the Breaking of the Vessels: fragments of great lights within kelipas nogah, which can be raised to holiness. He ends with the Rambam and Ramban, Torah immunity and the Chazon Ish.

en: An am ha'aretz who cannot learn receives only the general punishment for idle talk, but a talmid chacham who wastes his time transgresses bittul Torah, which has a special punishment of its own.

Torah must be learned lishmah, for its own sake, while secular wisdom is permitted only as a means, such as medicine to heal people or a skill to earn a livelihood, never for the sake of the wisdom itself.
Studying secular wisdom for its own sake is worse than idle talk such as baseball, because idle talk comes from the middos while secular wisdom defiles Chabad, the higher faculties of the soul.
Secular wisdom comes from fragments of Chabad that fell in the Breaking of the Vessels; it belongs to kelipas nogah and can therefore be raised to holiness.
Only those with great Torah attainment, like the Rambam and Ramban, are immune to the harm in secular wisdom and may use it for Torah; the Gedolei Yisrael knew such wisdom from the Torah itself.

title.en: Idle talk: the am ha'aretz and the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that forbidden speech belongs to the three impure kelipos and needs Gehinnom to cleanse it. He explains that an am ha'aretz who cannot learn is punished only generally, that today's untaught Jews are anusim who cannot be blamed for the delay of the redemption, and that a talmid chacham who talks idly transgresses bittul Torah.

title.en: The special punishment for bittul Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the kaf hakela, where two angels toss the soul back and forth, is not enough to cleanse bittul Torah; it is a positive commandment like others, yet worse, so it has a special punishment beyond the general one. He contrasts the Gehinnom of fire, for active sins that generate heat, with the Gehinnom of snow, for passive failure to do mitzvos.

title.en: Torah lishmah versus secular wisdom as a means

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tanya's distinction: Torah must be learned lishmah and not as a tool, while secular wisdom may be learned only shelo lishmah, for a purpose such as medicine or a livelihood. Learning it to become wise, like the Greek philosophers, is forbidden, and for a talmid chacham it is worse because he could have learned Torah.

title.en: Why secular wisdom is worse than baseball talk

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why studying secular wisdom is worse than idle talk about baseball. Such talk is empty and comes from a passion in the middos, so it defiles only the middos of the animal soul, whereas wisdom with real substance defiles Chabad, which is above the middos, and the blemish is far greater.

title.en: The Breaking of the Vessels and the kings of Edom

summary.en: Citing the Ramchal in Derech Hashem, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem's light was too great for the vessels, which cracked, and their fragments became the kelipos. He reads the kings of Edom at the end of Vayishlach: of the first seven it says 'he died', while of the eighth, Hadar, it does not, and his wife is named; he illustrates the pattern of giver and receiver with the image of a fern.

title.en: Giver and receiver: fragments of Chabad

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all of creation is built on giver and receiver, male and female, in time, space and soul. When the vessels, the receivers, were too small they broke; with Hadar a wife is named, a world with vessels that could receive and endure. The kelipos formed from the earlier worlds come from very great lights, so secular wisdom is the fallen fragments of Chabad.

title.en: Greek wisdom, kelipas nogah and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that secular wisdom is not from the three impure kelipos but from kelipas nogah, and can be used for good. Greek wisdom was wisdom for its own sake and defiled the 'oils', which are Chabad; its basic principle of not accepting what one cannot understand is fear, not science. Yavan oppressed the Jews in Eretz Yisrael, and Chanukah's mehadrin min hamehadrin relates to Hadar, the eighth king.

title.en: Questions on the purpose of the Breaking

summary.en: Answering listeners' questions, the Mashgiach compares the Breaking of the Vessels to a hava amina in the Gemara, which has holiness even though it is rejected, and says its purpose was to create a world of free choice. The kelipah keeps only a residue of life, which Hashem wants it to have, and he connects this to drinking on Purim; the true reason for the Breaking will be known when Moshiach comes.

title.en: The Tanya's words and the Rambam and Ramban

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's lines that secular wisdom defiles the Chabad of the G-dly soul and is from kelipas nogah, so it can still serve holiness. He explains why the Rambam and Ramban engaged in it, to bring out the beauty of the Torah, and stresses that the Tanya names them because only someone great in Torah is protected from its harm.

title.en: Immunity before approaching secular wisdom

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the higher, more dangerous kelipah of secular wisdom to the nations whose land is off limits now, since overcoming it needs greater strength than the middos. Only people like the Rambam and Ramban were immunized; even innocent subjects like medicine are taught today mixed with heresy such as evolution, so one must be well prepared.

title.en: Wisdom from the Torah: the Chazon Ish

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Gedolei Yisrael knew the sciences from the Torah, as the Ramban writes in his introduction, and tells how great neurosurgeons consulted the Chazon Ish, who mapped out brain surgery and said he knew it from the Torah. He closes by answering a listener's question about Hadar, the eighth king.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Kedoshim, the Mashgiach brings a vort of the Chasam Sofer that Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, and gathers the reasons for joy: the parsha, the day of Sefirah and the bris itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a vort of the Chasam Sofer: the first letters of the passuk about Moshe telling the festivals of Hashem to the Jewish people spell 'my mother' and 'my father', because Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, who teach him and instill good middos, as parents do for a child. He says he wanted to repeat it because the souls of forebears come to a simcha, and a descendant of the Chasam Sofer is at this bris. He then recalls that the companions of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rejoiced at Parshas Kedoshim, on which most of the Torah depends, since a Jew rejoices in whatever brings him closeness to Hashem. A bris brings that closeness, and this one coincides with Kedoshim, with a day of Sefirah linked to milah, and with the day's word in Lamenatzeach, 'yismechu'. He closes with blessings of joy for the parents, for Klal Yisrael and for the redemption.

en: Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, teaching him and giving him good middos.
The companions of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rejoiced when Parshas Kedoshim was read.
A Jew rejoices in what brings him closeness to Hashem, and every bris brings such closeness.
This bris joins several joys: the parsha, the day of Sefirah, the day's word 'yismechu', and the bris itself.

candidateTopics: Shabbos and the festivals as parents

title.en: Shabbos as father and mother; joy of Kedoshim and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's vort that Shabbos and the festivals are a Jew's father and mother, recalls the joy of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's companions at Parshas Kedoshim, and connects the bris to the parsha, the day of Sefirah and its word 'yismechu', ending with blessings for the parents and Klal Yisrael.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the festivals and the mitzvah of milah lift a Jew above the level of the tribes to the root of the Avos, and sees a sign in a bris that falls in the week of Parshas Emor, with its chapter of the festivals.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach describes the Avos as the trunk of the tree and the tribes as its branches. Each tribe has its own portion in Eretz Yisrael, and the mitzvos are spread over the land, but some things stand above the tribes, such as Yerushalayim. The three festivals correspond to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, so when Jews go up to Yerushalayim, where the tribes ascend, they rise above their tribal root to the root of the Avos. Milah too is above the tribes: it is the covenant of Avraham Avinu, and after his milah Hashem appeared to him, a revelation of 'seeing' tied to the command that every male appear on the festivals. A bris in the week of Parshas Emor, with its chapter of the festivals, is therefore a sign of an elevated bris that binds all present to the Avos. He blesses the child to enter Torah, chuppah and good deeds, and that his merit join that of Klal Yisrael.

en: The Avos are the trunk of the tree and the tribes are its branches, each with its own portion in Eretz Yisrael.
The three festivals correspond to the Avos, so on them Jews rise above the root of the tribes to the root of the Avos.
Milah is above the tribes; it is the covenant of Avraham Avinu and binds to the root of the Avos.
A bris in the week of the festivals' chapter is a sign of an elevated bris that binds everyone present to the Avos.

candidateTopics: the three festivals and the Avos

title.en: Milah and the festivals: above the tribes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the tribes are branches of the Avos, that the festivals and the going up to Yerushalayim lift Jews to the root of the Avos, and that milah, the covenant of Avraham, does the same. He sees the bris in the week of Parshas Emor as a sign of an elevated bris and closes with blessings for the child and the family.

catalogTitle: ביאור האיך התאוות באים מהלב אל המח. מלחמת שני מלכים על הגוף.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 9, the Mashgiach explains that desires rise from the heart's left chamber to the mind while holiness starts in the mind and comes down to the heart, and that the two souls wage war like two kings over the small city of the body.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the two inclinations and reads Tanya chapter 9: the animal soul sits in the blood of the heart's left chamber. With the example of a person who sees an ice cream, he shows that desire begins in the heart and sends the mind to carry it out, while love and fear of Hashem must begin with the mind contemplating Hashem's greatness and only then move the heart. He supports this from the contrast between David speaking to his heart and Haman speaking in his heart, and explains the prohibition of blood as not strengthening one's own animal soul. He then shows the same order in the blessings before Krias Shema, discusses why the Tanya places anger last and how rarely anger is truly for Heaven, and describes the war of the two kings over the body, with Avraham and the four kings and the war against chametz. He ends with the godly soul's wish to rule alone and the pleasure that lies in the mind.

en: The animal soul and the yetzer hara are seated in the blood of the heart's left chamber, which carries the body's biological life.
Physical desire starts in the heart and sends a message up to the mind, which only works out how to get what the heart wants.
In holiness the order is reversed: nobody naturally desires to learn or daven, so it must begin with the mind contemplating Hashem's greatness, which then brings love and fear into the heart.
Blood is forbidden even where it is not brought on the altar, because the blood is the soul, and eating it would add to a person's own animal soul.
The two souls are two kings waging war over the body, a small city of 248 inhabitants, each wanting all the limbs to follow its rule.
The godly soul wants to rule alone, with the body as nullified to it as a chariot to its rider, so that not even a passing thought serves the other side.

mind and heart in serving Hashem
anger for the sake of Heaven
war of the two kings over the body

title.en: The animal soul seated in the left chamber

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the godly soul and the yetzer hara and begins Tanya chapter 9: the animal soul is in the heart's left chamber, in the blood that carries biological life. He recalls that the midos are called 'double' since they can serve good or bad, and asks why the intellect is not called so.

title.en: Desire rises from heart to mind

summary.en: With the example of a person who sees an ice cream, the Mashgiach explains that desire starts in the heart and the mind only implements it, while love and fear of Hashem must start with the mind and trickle down to the heart's right chamber. A listener asks about the drive for secular wisdom, and the Mashgiach says most intellectual pursuit comes from pride.

title.en: David's heart, Haman's heart, and the blood

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash contrasting David, who spoke to his heart, with Haman, who spoke in his heart, and Rashi on Beshalach and Yisro, to show that the wicked begin with the heart and the righteous with the mind. He then explains the prohibition of blood: the blood is the soul, and eating it would strengthen one's own animal soul. He wonders why the Tanya changes the order of the midos and leaves it for later.

title.en: The godly soul in the brain

summary.en: Continuing the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that the desires rise from the heart to the brain only to be implemented, while the godly soul's seat is the brain, which he connects to the tefillin of the head and of the arm. Love of Hashem burns in the right chamber like flames, but it comes from deep thought in the mind, since the mind itself is cold logic.

title.en: The order of the blessings before Shema

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same order in davening: the blessing of Yotzer describes the vast creation and the awe of the angels, which brings fear, then Ahavah Rabbah brings love, and only then comes Shema. He brings a remark of the Rebbe Rashab that by Ahavah Rabbah the angels are no longer mentioned, and adds that contemplating Hashem's glory brings joy of the heart.

title.en: Why anger is placed last

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests that the Tanya, being about avodas Hashem, first lists the midos the mind stimulates for good and puts anger at the end, since anger is rarely a tool for serving Hashem. In a discussion with listeners he says anger purely for Heaven is reserved for very special people, and that anger at others usually hides insecurity or pride in one's own group.

title.en: Two kings and the small city

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each of the two powers strives to conquer the other, and reads the body as the small city of Koheles with 248 inhabitants, over which two kings wage war. He links this to Avraham's war with the four kings as the four klipos, and to Pesach, bringing the Radbaz's answer to Tosafos' question why chametz is treated so strictly: chametz is the yetzer hara.

title.en: The godly soul wants to rule alone

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the godly soul's wish that all the limbs be under its discipline and nullified to it, like a beast of burden to its owner and, more, like a chariot to its rider. It wants not even a passing thought for the other king, as Edom refused even to let Israel pass through its land.

title.en: Overflowing love and the pleasure of the mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the intellectual fear and the love that come from the mind should fill the heart's right chamber until it overflows into the left and conquers it, as David did. He describes Ahavah Rabbah and the higher love of delight, whose source is the pleasure of the mind in grasping a deep idea, and discusses with a listener how this differs from the satisfaction of accomplishment, with the example of a man alone on an island.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Sefilah Yesod Malchus

oneLiner.en: At a bris of twins on Yesod shebeMalchus, the Mashgiach explains that this day of the Omer completes the tikkun of Yesod, a sign that the child is prepared to become a tzaddik, and ties the twins to the mazal of Sivan and Matan Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by mentioning the custom not to take a haircut during the days of Sefiras HaOmer and how practice differs between places. He notes that there is a deeper reason, but in simple terms one can explain that by Yesod shebeMalchus the Omer count has already passed through the Yesod of every middah, so the whole tikkun of Yesod is complete. A bris, which is in Yesod, held on Yesod shebeMalchus is therefore a good sign that the child is prepared to be a tzaddik and to grow in Torah and yiras Shamayim. It is also a great preparation for Matan Torah. Since this is a bris of twins, the Mashgiach adds that the mazal of the month of Sivan, the month of receiving the Torah, is te'omim, twins, as the Bnei Yissaschar and other sefarim bring. He closes with brachos for the children and the parents.

en: By Yesod shebeMalchus the Omer count has passed through the Yesod of every middah, so the tikkun of Yesod is complete.
A bris, which is in Yesod, on Yesod shebeMalchus is a sign that the child is prepared to become a great tzaddik.
A bris on this day is a great preparation for Matan Torah.
The mazal of Sivan, the month of receiving the Torah, is twins, which makes a bris of twins on this day especially fitting.

candidateTopics: twins and the mazal of Sivan

title.en: A bris of twins on Yesod shebeMalchus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that by Yesod shebeMalchus the tikkun of Yesod is complete, so a bris on that day signals the child is prepared to be a tzaddik and prepares for Matan Torah; he ties the twins to the mazal of Sivan and closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Emor, the Mashgiach explains why the parsha of the kohanim is the parsha Eliyahu HaNavi will expound, and connects it to Eliyahu at every bris and to a young father who held fast to Yiddishkeit.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the week's haftorah from Yechezkel about the kohanim, the bnei Tzadok, who kept Hashem's charge when the rest of Yisrael strayed; they kept up the Jewish mesorah, and they will be the ones who draw close to Hashem in the days of Moshiach. The haftorah ends with the prohibition for kohanim to eat neveilah and treifah, and the Gemara asks why kohanim are singled out; Rabbi Yochanan answers that Eliyahu will expound this parsha. The Mashgiach explains that at the geulah the spirit of impurity will be removed and even forbidden things will become kosher, as the Midrash says of the chazir, but the kohanim, as higher Jews, will still not eat them. Every Jew has his own letter in the Torah, and Emor is Eliyahu's parsha. Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek and malach habris, comes to every bris, so a bris in Emor for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit is a special segulah. He closes with brachos.

en: The kohanim, bnei Tzadok, kept Hashem's charge and the Jewish mesorah when the rest of Yisrael strayed, and they will draw close to Hashem in the days of Moshiach.
Eliyahu will expound the parsha of neveilah and treifah for kohanim because at the geulah even forbidden things will become kosher, yet the kohanim will still not eat them.
Every Jew has his own letter in the Torah, where his learning shines and his chiddushim come, and Emor is Eliyahu's parsha.
A bris in the week of Emor, for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit, is a special segulah, since Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek and malach habris, comes to every bris.

forbidden foods becoming permitted at the geulah
each jew's letter in the torah

title.en: The bnei Tzadok and the parsha Eliyahu will expound

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the kohanim, bnei Tzadok, who stayed loyal when Yisrael strayed, then brings the Gemara that Eliyahu will expound the prohibition of neveilah and treifah for kohanim, and explains it: at the geulah forbidden things will become kosher, but the kohanim will not eat them.

title.en: Eliyahu's parsha and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that every Jew has a letter in the Torah and that Emor is Eliyahu's parsha; Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek of the bris benching, is the malach habris, so this bris for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit is a special segulah. He closes with brachos to hear Eliyahu's derasha at the geulah.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Laag Beomer

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach explains that being counted by Moshe Rabbeinu, like being seen by Eliyahu HaNavi at a bris, is itself a great blessing, and that the last, fallen generation of 'Bnei Naftali' is helped from Above when it serves Hashem with mesiras nefesh.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the week's parsha: every tribe is counted 'livnei', with a lamed, except Naftali. He brings the Chasam Sofer: since Naftali was counted last, its number was already known, so its count served only the purpose the Ramban describes, that each Jew came before Moshe and Aharon to be seen and blessed. He then explains why Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris: a father who cuts his own child with joy needs help from Above, and Eliyahu, who was moser nefesh for the bris in the episode of Zimri, comes to help. Being seen by him is a great good, like being seen by Moshe. The child is named after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Our generation, the last and 'fallen' one, is Bnei Naftali, and whoever holds on to Torah with mesiras nefesh is helped by Hashem. He closes with blessings.

en: Naftali's count lacks the lamed because, as the last tribe, its number was already known, so it was counted only so that its people would come before Moshe Rabbeinu and be blessed.
Being counted by Moshe and Aharon was a great good for each Jew: Moshe looked at him, asked how he was doing and blessed him.
Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris to help the father, who needs great strength and help from Above to cut his own child with joy.
Whoever wants to serve Hashem is helped: angels and souls of tzaddikim come to help him, and above all Hashem Himself.
Our generation, the last one, is 'Bnei Naftali', a fallen generation in which holding on to Torah and mitzvos takes mesiras nefesh, and Hashem helps whoever does so.

help from Above in serving Hashem

title.en: Why Naftali is counted without a lamed

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that in the parsha's census every tribe is counted 'livnei' except Naftali. He brings the Chasam Sofer and the Ramban: Naftali's number was already known, so it was counted only so that its people would come before Moshe Rabbeinu, be looked at and blessed.

title.en: Why Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a father who cuts his child with joy needs help from Above, and Eliyahu, who was moser nefesh for the holiness of the bris in the episode of Zimri, comes to help. Being seen by Eliyahu is a great good, like being seen by Moshe; he blesses the child to enter Torah, chuppah and good deeds with the same mesiras nefesh and joy.

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the last generation, and blessings

summary.en: The child is named after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and the Mashgiach brings the Midrash Pinchas that the soul whose name is given comes to the bris. He explains that the last generation is Bnei Naftali, a fallen generation, and that whoever holds on to Torah in it with mesiras nefesh receives help from Above, and closes with blessings for the child, the family and all present.

catalogTitle: רצון הנפש האלוקות הוא שהגוף יהיה בטל לה לגמרי. חילוק בין אהבה עזה לאהבה רבה. רצון הפנימי של היצה"ר הוא שיהיה מנוצח.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter nine, the Mashgiach explains that the G-dly soul wants the whole body to be utterly nullified to it, distinguishes strong love (ahavah azah) from great love (ahavah rabbah), and shows that the inner wish of the yetzer hara is to be conquered.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach rereads the end of Tanya chapter nine, opening with the verse in Koheles about a small city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man: the city is the body, and the two souls are two kings fighting over it. The G-dly soul wants every limb to be nullified to it like a pen to the writer or a chariot to its rider, with mind, heart, speech and action given over to Hashem. He explains that the right chamber of the heart should overflow into the left and transform its desires, and distinguishes passing strong love from great love, a delight felt in the mind itself. He describes tzaddikim whose every word and movement served Hashem, with examples from Daniel, Yosef, Pharaoh's reversed heart, the Satmar Rav, the Arizal and the Maggid. He ends with the Zohar's parable showing that the yetzer hara's inner wish is to be overcome.

en: The small city in Koheles is the body, and the G-dly soul and the animal soul are two kings each fighting to rule it alone.
The G-dly soul wants every limb to be nullified to it without asking why, like a pen to the writer or a chariot to its rider.
Ahavah azah is a strong love that can come and go, while ahavah rabbah fills the heart to the brim so that no room is left for the yetzer hara.
Ahavah rabbah is a delight felt in the mind itself, higher than any feeling of the heart, like the joy of finally grasping a hard idea.
In great tzaddikim even ordinary speech and every movement of the hand were directed to Hashem.
The yetzer hara is in the King's service, and its deep inner wish is that a person master and conquer it.

the yetzer hara's wish to be conquered

title.en: The small city in Koheles

summary.en: The Mashgiach starts the page over and reads the verse in Koheles about a small city besieged by a great king and saved by a poor wise man whom nobody remembers. He explains that the city is the body and the poor wise man is the good inclination.

title.en: Two kings and the nullified body

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's image of the two souls as two kings warring over the body. The G-dly soul wants every limb nullified to it like a pen to the writer and a chariot to its rider, and the three chambers of the mind filled with understanding of Hashem's greatness that gives birth to fear and love.

title.en: The right chamber overflows into the left

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the ultimate level: the yetzer hara driven out entirely, so that the love in the right chamber of the heart burns like a flame and overflows into the left chamber, overpowering and transforming its desires into love of Hashem, as in serving Hashem with both inclinations.

title.en: Ahavah azah and ahavah rabbah

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes strong love, which comes and goes, from great love, which fills the heart and leaves no room for the yetzer hara. He explains that usually the mind arouses the heart, but in ahavah rabbah the mind itself feels a delight in grasping Hashem, like the thrill of solving a hard problem, and this transforms all the emotions.

title.en: Tzaddikim who speak only to Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes tzaddikim who feel no worldly pleasure and whose speech, even to people, is directed to Hashem. He notes that the Tanya is a book for beinonim, who should still know what a tzaddik is, and brings Daniel speaking to the king and Yosef's brothers' plea as words that were really addressed to Hashem, a holy language Pharaoh could not learn.

title.en: Pharaoh's heart was liver

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains how Pharaoh withstood plague after plague: the process ran in reverse, the left chamber overflowing into the right. He brings the Midrash on 'kaved lev Paroh' with the parable of the lion, the donkey and the fox, and explains that the liver is the seat of the yetzer hara, while a tzaddik's heart is a real heart.

title.en: The Satmar Rav: a rasha has no heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a vort he heard from the Satmar Rav on 'all hearts fear You'. He explains that Hashem has no body, but the eye, mouth and heart said of Hashem are powers, and man, made in the image of G-d, has physical organs that are a likeness of them; a rasha's heart and eye do not deserve the name, since they do not do what a heart and eye are for.

title.en: Tzaddikim beyond their generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the perfect tzaddik whose whole day is bound to Hashem and explains that, though generations decline, sometimes a soul of earlier times is sent down, as with the Arizal, the Ba'al Shem Tov and his talmidim, and even the Vilna Gaon. He tells of the Maggid, who noticed a moved snuffbox and who held his hand still for hours because he found no holy reason to move it.

title.en: The yetzer hara wants to be conquered

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the yetzer hara, though the opposite of the G-dly soul, is for a person's good: its inner wish is to be conquered. He brings the Zohar's parable of the king who hired a harlot to test his son, and explains the angel of Esav fighting Yaakov on the night before his turn to sing shirah: his shirah was to be overpowered, just as the sun's shirah is its motion, which is why Yehoshua told it to be silent.

title.en: Questions: a bigger tzaddik, a bigger yetzer

summary.en: Listeners ask questions about the decline of the generations and the yetzer hara of a tzaddik. The Mashgiach answers that there must always be a balance, so a bigger tzaddik has a bigger yetzer, until he reaches the level of David, who said his heart was hollow within him.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Sivan, the Mashgiach distinguishes two brissos, Hashem's covenant of the soul with Avraham and the bris milah that is its sign, and explains that in Sivan, the month of Matan Torah, the covenant between Klal Yisrael and Hashem is strengthened.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Midrash that in Megillas Rus every passuk but eight begins with a vav, hinting that Rus accepted the mitzvah of milah. He notes that Avraham received his new name before his milah, though a name is usually given after it. To explain, he distinguishes two brissos: first, Hashem's covenant with Avraham, a bond of the neshamah that ties every Jew to Hashem and does not depend on the flesh, as the Mishnah in Nedarim says that a Jew is called circumcised even if he is not, and a non-Jew uncircumcised even if he is; for this Avraham received his name. Afterwards came the os bris, the bris milah, as a sign of that covenant. A woman shares in the first bris, and that is what Rus took on. A bris in Sivan, when Klal Yisrael came to Sinai and their covenant with Hashem was strengthened, is a great chizuk to feel bound to Hashem, like Avraham, the first of the believers. He closes with brachos.

en: There are two brissos: Hashem's covenant with Avraham, a bond of the neshamah, and the bris milah, which is its sign.
The covenant of the neshamah does not depend on the flesh: a Jew is called circumcised even if he is not, and a non-Jew uncircumcised even if he is.
Avraham received his name for the first covenant, which is why it came before his milah.
A woman also belongs to the covenant of Avraham, and this is what Rus accepted, as hinted by the eight pesukim that do not begin with a vav.
In Sivan, when Yisrael came to Sinai, their covenant with Hashem was strengthened, so a bris in Sivan is a great chizuk to feel bound to Hashem.

title.en: Avraham's name and the covenant of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Rus accepted milah, asks why Avraham was named before his milah, and answers with two brissos: a covenant of the neshamah that binds every Jew to Hashem regardless of the flesh, as the Mishnah in Nedarim shows, and the later os bris in the flesh.

title.en: Rus, Sivan and strengthening the covenant

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rus took on the covenant of Avraham, which a woman shares, and that a bris in Sivan, when Yisrael's covenant with Hashem was strengthened at Sinai, is a chizuk to feel bound to Hashem like Avraham, the first of the believers; he closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shavuos the Mashgiach explains, from the end of Megillas Rus, why Oved was given that name: he carried a difficult heritage that he had to refine through hard work, and that is the blessing given to the newborn child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the blessing in Megillas Rus, 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael', which the Targum reads as a wish that the child be counted among the tzaddikim of Israel, and a Midrash that the last eight pesukim of the megillah correspond to the bris on the eighth day. He asks why the megillah repeats the genealogy from Peretz after naming Oved as the grandfather of Dovid. Bringing the Arizal, he explains that Oved carried the soul of Machlon, returned through yibum, and before that the history of Er through Peretz. This is why he was called Oved: the Targum says he served Hashem with a whole heart, but many did that; Oved had to work hard on himself to refine what he was born with. Rus, too, labored all her life on her traits, which is why the neighbors named the child. The Mashgiach ends with the eighth day, above nature, its link to Shavuos, and blessings for the child.

en: The blessing 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael' at the end of Megillas Rus is, per the Targum, a wish that the child be among the tzaddikim of Israel, and it was said at Oved's bris.
Oved carried the soul of Machlon, brought back through yibum, and through Peretz also the history of Er, which needed rectifying.
He was called Oved because he had to work hard on himself to refine what he was born with, unlike a tzaddik who serves Hashem easily out of a good heart.
Rus, born a daughter of the king of Moav, labored all her life to refine her traits, and the neighbors named the child because she would not, remembering her past.
Milah on the eighth day is above nature, which runs in sevens, and it is linked to the Torah given as the eighth week begins.

title.en: Oved's bris and the souls of Machlon and Er

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael', the Targum's reading of it, and a Midrash tying the megillah's last eight pesukim to the bris on the eighth day. He asks why the genealogy from Peretz is repeated and brings the Arizal that Oved carried the soul of Machlon through yibum, and that Er stood behind Peretz.

title.en: Why he was called Oved

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks, with the Targum that Oved served Hashem with a whole heart, why only he was called by that name. He answers that the histories of Machlon and Peretz merged in him, so he had to work hard on himself, and this made him the forebear of Yishai; milah, too, removes the bad a person is born with.

title.en: Rus, the neighbors' name, and the eighth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rus labored all her life to refine her traits, so she would not name the child, and the neighbors comforted her and blessed him to be an oved. He ties milah on the eighth day, above nature, to the Torah given at Shavuos, and ends with blessings for the child.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz the Mashgiach explains that, as milah removes the orlah to reveal the holiness beneath, the dark days of Tamuz hide great light, and contrasts milah, holiness above understanding, with tefillin, the peak of understanding.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach notes that the bris falls on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz, at the start of the period that the navi says will turn into days of joy. Everything in the soul exists in time: the bris kodesh is the greatest holiness, covered by an orlah, and a Jew's work is to remove it; so too Tamuz, the brightest month, is covered, and through toil in Torah and avodah one finds the Shechinah 'bein hametzarim'. Sefer Yetzirah links Tamuz to the letter ches, the first ches in the Torah is choshech, darkness, and Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or'. A child circumcised on such a day is suited to reveal that light. From the Gemara on 'sasson' as milah and 'yekar' as tefillin, he explains milah as holiness above daas, given before a child understands, and tefillin as the peak of daas. Everyone at a bris should take this to heart, and he closes with blessings for redemption.

en: Just as the holiness of the bris is covered by an orlah that must be removed, the bright month of Tamuz is covered, and its light is revealed through toil in Torah and avodah.
Tamuz is linked to the letter ches, whose first appearance in the Torah is choshech, darkness; Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or', so the darkness turns to light.
A child circumcised on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz is suited to toil in Torah and avodah and to reveal the light of Torah and of Klal Yisrael.
Milah is given to an infant because the holiness of a Jew, rooted in Avraham, is above daas; tefillin, by contrast, is the peak of daas.
Jews have two kinds of holiness: what Hashem gives them, and what they work for themselves, represented by milah and tefillin.

title.en: Tamuz: great light covered like the orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the bris falls on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz, whose fasts the navi says will become festivals. As the holiness of the bris is covered by an orlah, the brightest month is covered, and through toil in Torah and avodah one finds the Shechinah 'bein hametzarim'.

title.en: The letter ches: turning darkness to light

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Sefer Yetzirah that Tamuz is ruled by the letter ches, the first ches in the Torah being choshech, and shows that Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or'. A child circumcised on Rosh Chodesh, which holds the whole month, is suited to reveal the light under the darkness; he blesses the parents.

title.en: Sasson and yekar: milah and tefillin

summary.en: From the Gemara that 'sasson' is milah and 'yekar' is tefillin, the Mashgiach asks why milah is not delayed until the child can do it knowingly, and answers that a Jew's holiness is above daas, while tefillin are the peak of daas. Everyone at a bris should be stirred to bring that root into daas, and he closes with blessings for the geulah.

catalogTitle: יש צדיק שמדריגתו למעלה מדורו. ביאור חילוק בין צדיק וטוב לו לצדיק ורע לו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 10, the Mashgiach explains the difference between the tzaddik who has transformed his evil into good and the tzaddik in whom a hidden residue of evil remains, and describes the special tzaddikim, above their generation, who no longer have a yetzer hara.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 10 and says that now the Ba'al HaTanya begins answering the questions of chapter one: what are tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo. There are tzaddikim with no yetzer hara, like David HaMelech, whose heart was 'chalal', empty. He describes the special tzaddikim sent close to the days of Moshiach, like the Arizal and the tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era, who remembered earlier gilgulim, and explains why ordinary people forget: to keep their free choice. Pharaoh lost his choice as a punishment, and a story about Czar Nicholas shows that even a rasha's downfall can serve Hashem. The tzaddik who is not complete drives his evil away, but like David leaving Avimelech, it goes off on its own and can return. The complete tzaddik has transformed his evil and despises worldly pleasure, as the Apter Rav did, except where enjoyment itself is the mitzvah, as with eating matzah.

en: There are tzaddikim who have rendered their yetzer hara null and void; David HaMelech said his heart was 'chalal', empty of it, and so he no longer had free choice in that sense.

Close to the days of Moshiach Hashem sends exceptional tzaddikim, above the normal descent of the generations, like the Arizal and the tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era, to keep Klal Yisrael going.
Ordinary people do not remember their earlier gilgulim so that they keep their free choice; perfect tzaddikim, who live only to guide others, may remember.
The tzaddik who is not complete has driven the evil out of the left chamber of the heart, but it was not transformed; a tiny residue remains, subdued and nullified.
The complete tzaddik's evil has been transformed into good, so he despises worldly pleasures that are not for the service of Hashem.
The complete tzaddik hates evil for two reasons: Hashem hates it, and his heart is so filled with love of Hashem that no room is left for any other love.

title.en: Tzaddikim with no yetzer hara

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 10 and says the Ba'al HaTanya now begins answering the questions of chapter one about tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo. He explains that some tzaddikim have no yetzer hara, as David HaMelech said his heart was 'chalal', which means empty, like chillul Shabbos empties Shabbos of its kedushah.

title.en: Exceptional tzaddikim near Moshiach's days

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that although the generations grow smaller, close to Moshiach's days there are tzaddikim beyond the normal descent, like the Arizal, whom Reb Chaim Vital describes as grasping more than the nevi'im. He explains that such people are needed because the state of Klal Yisrael today is so low, and he brings the Ohr HaChaim on falling into the fiftieth gate of impurity.

title.en: Tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the era of the Ba'al Shem Tov, when great neshamos came down and spoke openly of their earlier gilgulim: the Ohev Yisrael of Apt and the Yismach Moshe, who remembered Matan Torah and the dispute of Korach and told his grandson he had stayed neutral. He adds that Korach was a great man with ruach hakodesh, and mentions Reb Shmelke of Nikolsburg and his brother in Mezritch.

title.en: Why we forget: preserving free choice

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that ordinary people do not remember earlier gilgulim because their task is to fight the yetzer hara, and remembering would remove their free choice. Perfect tzaddikim have finished their own task and live only to guide others, so they may remember; he laments that today there is no such leadership.

title.en: Pharaoh, Czar Nicholas and the rasha's purpose

summary.en: In reverse, Pharaoh lost his free choice as a punishment he brought on himself. The Mashgiach tells how a tzaddik explained why Czar Nicholas died a natural death: he was too wicked to merit a Kiddush Hashem through his downfall, whereas Pharaoh did merit it. He brings the passuk that even the rasha was created for the day of evil, and contrasts David HaMelech, who sanctified Hashem with his life.

title.en: The tzaddik in whom evil remains

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out the four levels the Tanya will explain: the complete and incomplete tzaddik and the complete and incomplete rasha. He reads how a person fights until he drives the evil out of the left chamber of the heart, yet it was not transformed; a tiny subdued residue remains, which is the Gemara's tzaddik v'ra lo, and the tzaddik thinks it is gone. He then asks whether the Ba'al HaTanya uses a passuk merely as poetic language.

title.en: Vayegarshehu vayelech: the evil that leaves by itself

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains melitza, using a passuk out of context, and says the Ba'al HaTanya means every word exactly. He tells how David feigned madness before Avimelech, and points to the extra word in the passuk: Avimelech thought he drove David out, but David left of his own will. So too the incomplete tzaddik thinks he has driven out the yetzer hara, but it left on its own and is ready to attack again.

title.en: The complete tzaddik and the Apter Rav's matzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the complete tzaddik the evil was transformed into good, so he despises worldly pleasures not for the service of Hashem. He tells of the Apter Rav, who could eat an entire goose after a feast, yet at the end of his life said all food tasted like dust to him except the matzah of the Seder night.

title.en: Achila means enjoyment: the body feels the mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests that the mitzvah with matzah is achila, which means enjoying the food, and brings a proof that one must eat it with appetite. He adds that enjoyment leaves a mark on the body: the Gemara holds one who is mis'asek with forbidden fats liable because he had pleasure, and on Pesach the body itself is to be sanctified by feeling the mitzvah.

title.en: Two reasons the tzaddik hates evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every desire comes from the sitra achra, and the complete tzaddik hates it for two reasons: Hashem hates it, and his heart is so full of love for Hashem that no room remains for another love, as in 'ohavei Hashem sinu ra'. He raises the question of how one can also love a fellow Jew, and answers that one loves the part of G-d in him, so the love is not divided.

title.en: Tachlis sinah: hatred and revulsion

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings David HaMelech's words that he hates the resha'im with utmost hatred and asks Hashem to search his heart, showing that the measure of his love is the measure of his hatred of evil. He distinguishes mius, revulsion felt toward objects, from sinah, hatred of people, and explains that the tzaddik's soul is revolted by evil as the senses are by spoiled food. He stops at the complete tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Behaaloscha, the Mashgiach speaks of the kindling of the menorah and explains that while Eliyahu HaNavi's emissaries come to every bris, at a special bris like this one Eliyahu comes himself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a theme from Parshas Behaaloscha, the menorah and its daily kindling and preparation. He then turns to the bris itself: Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, but usually it is his emissaries who come, while at a truly special bris Eliyahu comes himself, and he says today's bris is such a one. He speaks of the importance of a bris in a family that has lived through hard times, and closes with blessings that the parents raise the child to Torah and good deeds.

en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah of Parshas Behaaloscha, its kindling and the preparing of its lamps.
Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, but at most only his emissaries come, while at a very special bris he comes himself.
The Mashgiach says that today's bris is such a bris, to which Eliyahu comes himself.
A bris in a family that has gone through hard times is an especially precious bris.

title.en: The menorah, and Eliyahu at a special bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah of Behaaloscha, then explains that Eliyahu's emissaries come to every bris but Eliyahu himself comes to a special bris, as he says today's is. He speaks of the worth of a bris in a family that has known hardship and closes with blessings for the child and parents.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Behaaloscha, the Mashgiach explains Rashi's praise that Aharon 'did not change': he chose the lamps, which bring Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, over the ketores, which brings wealth, every day for forty years, and wishes that this home merit both together.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi on 'vaya'as ken Aharon' in this week's parsha: it tells Aharon's praise, that he did not change. He explains that in the Beis HaMikdash the one who merited to offer the ketores had a promise of wealth, while the avodah of preparing the lamps brought the merit of Torah and of sons who are talmidei chachamim. Aharon, who could pick any avodah he wished, took the lamps every day, and since one person cannot do both, he gave up the ketores. The Mashgiach asks why, in forty years in the desert, Aharon did not give up the lamps even one day to gain a little wealth, as a father needs to marry off children, and answers that this is his praise: he never changed. He then turns to the bris, where Torah is precious in the family, and blesses the father, the grandparents and the guests that the light of Torah shine from the home, together with greatness.

en: Rashi's words on 'vaya'as ken Aharon', that he did not change, are Aharon's praise for lighting the lamps every day.
The Mashgiach says that offering the ketores carried a promise of wealth, while the avodah of the lamps brought Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim.
Since one person cannot both prepare the lamps and offer the ketores, Aharon's daily choice of the lamps meant giving up the ketores.
The Mashgiach applies this to the bris: in this family Torah is precious, and he wishes that the light of Torah shine from the home.
