title.en: Aharon chose the lamps over the ketores

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Rashi's praise of Aharon that he did not change: he took the lamps, which bring Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, and gave up the ketores, which brings wealth, every day for forty years. He applies it to the family of the bris and closes with blessings for the father, the grandparents and the guests.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Balak, the Mashgiach explains that the parsha is named for the hidden spark of Moshiach in Balak, that the days of bein hametzarim hold great kedusha covered by an orlah, and that a bris now is a sign that Hashem will remove that orlah and bring the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why a parsha should be named after Balak. He explains that Balak usually falls just before the three weeks, and the holy sefarim say these days will become the greatest days, as Zechariah says the fasts will turn to joy; now they are covered by din. Where kedusha is greatest the kelipah is strongest, as the Sfas Emes says, in a person, in a place such as Eretz Yisrael, and in time. Hashem will come as the mohel and remove this orlah. Balak, a terrible kelipah, held a holy spark, for Chazal say he was the ancestor of Rus and so of Moshiach ben David; the parsha is named for that spark. Balak feared that the orlah would be removed and Moshiach revealed, but in the end the spark came out. A bris in this week is therefore a good sign, and the Mashgiach says that at such a bris Eliyahu HaNavi himself comes, and he blesses the family.

en: The days of bein hametzarim are destined to be the greatest days of the year, but now they are covered by din.
Where kedusha is greatest, the kelipah over it is strongest, and it must be cut away.
The parsha is named after Balak because of the holy spark in him, from which Moshiach ben David descends.
A bris in Parshas Balak is a good sign that Hashem will remove the orlah of these days and reveal their kedusha.
Eliyahu HaNavi, the herald of the geulah, comes to every bris, and to an important bris he comes himself.

title.en: Great kedusha covered by an orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a parsha is named after Balak, and explains that the coming days of bein hametzarim hold the greatest kedusha, now covered by din, because where kedusha is greatest the kelipah is strongest, in a person, a place and a time. Hashem will come as the mohel and remove the orlah.

title.en: Balak's hidden spark and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Balak held a spark of Moshiach, as the ancestor of Rus, and feared its revelation, yet it came out in the end; a bris in this week is a good sign of the geulah. He adds that Eliyahu HaNavi himself comes to an important bris and closes with blessings for the family.

catalogTitle: צדיק ורע לו - עוד יש לו שייכות אל הרע. “ראיתי בני עליה והמה מועטים” - זה צדיק וטוב לו. ביאור ענין יחוד קובהו"ש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapters 10 and 11, the Mashgiach explains the levels of tzaddikim, why the highest are called 'bnei aliyah', the meaning of uniting Hashem with the Shechinah, and the many levels of the 'rasha v'tov lo'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 10. A tzaddik who never sins but keeps a tiny residue of evil is a 'tzaddik she'eino gamur', and this level divides into countless levels; these are the 18,000 tzaddikim of the Gemara. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's 'bnei aliyah', who are few, transformed their evil into good. The Tanya gives a second reason for the name: they serve only for Hashem's need, not even to quench their own thirst for closeness. The Mashgiach explains 'l'shem yichud': the Shechinah in Klal Yisrael is the kallah, Hashem the chassan, and the tzaddik reunites them. He develops the pattern of mashpia and mekabel in creation, the Sitra Achra's temporary snatching of a destined union, Eretz Yisrael, and David and Bathsheba. Then, in chapter 11, he explains the 'rasha v'tov lo', why a thought of sin can be worse than a sin, and the many levels of this rasha.

en: A tzaddik who never sins but still has a dormant trace of evil is a tzaddik she'eino gamur, and the Mashgiach identifies these with the Gemara's 18,000 tzaddikim.
The 'bnei aliyah' whom Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai called few are those who transformed their evil into good and raised it to holiness.
A second reason for the name is that the bnei aliyah do everything only for Hashem's need, not for themselves, not even to satisfy their own thirst for closeness to Him.
Doing a mitzvah 'l'shem yichud' means uniting the Shechinah dwelling in Klal Yisrael, the kallah, with Hashem, the chassan, and so relieving the Shechinah of its exile.
A 'rasha v'tov lo' is a person whose good is temporarily subordinate to his evil at the moment he sins, but whose strong yetzer tov will bring him to teshuvah.
The rasha v'tov lo has countless levels, from one who slips once in ten years to one who sins several times a day and is full of regret.

title.en: The 18,000 tzaddikim and the few bnei aliyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the tzaddik gamur and the tzaddik who still carries a dormant trace of evil, whose level divides into countless levels. He brings the Gemara's 18,000 tzaddikim and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement that the bnei aliyah are few, and resolves them: the 18,000 still have a trace of evil, while Rabbi Shimon had none.

title.en: Turning darkness into light

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the first reason for the name bnei aliyah: they raise and transform their evil into good. He brings the Zohar about Rabbi Chiya, who could not enter Rabbi Shimon's chamber without having turned darkness into light, and notes that the Tanya, which calls itself a book for beinonim, describes this level only so the reader knows what he is not.

title.en: L'shem yichud: uniting chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the tzaddik who does nothing for himself, not even for Gan Eden or his own attachment to the Shechinah, and explains 'l'shem yichud': the Shechinah in Klal Yisrael is the kallah, Hashem the chassan, and through mitzvos the tzaddik reunites them and relieves the Shechinah of its exile. He reads 'chassid mitchased im kono' as kindness to Hashem's nest, and explains that acting for oneself would mean ego.

title.en: For Hashem's need, not to quench a thirst

summary.en: Reading the Tanya's text, the Mashgiach explains that the bnei aliyah serve for the need above, not to quench their own thirst for Hashem as in the passuk 'Hoy kol tzamei'. He brings the Tikkunei Zohar on the chassid and the Raya Mehemna's parable of a son who gives his life for his parents, then sums up the two explanations of bnei aliyah and notes that the Tanya's bracketed Kabbalistic passage unites them.

title.en: Mashpia and mekabel throughout creation

summary.en: To explain the yichud, the Mashgiach shows that all of creation comes as giver and receiver, sun and moon, day and night, as a parable for Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. The Sitra Achra tries to block this union and at times snatches the kallah away, but only temporarily, like a destined match taken by another, and like Eretz Yisrael, first held by Canaan and then returned to Klal Yisrael.

title.en: David, Bathsheba and the hidden union

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David and Bathsheba were the destined match of Adam and Chavah and the true parable of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, from whom Moshiach comes through Shlomo, and that David's desire was spiritual. Asked why it came about in such a roundabout way, he answers that the Satan always tries to block Moshiach's coming, so it is hidden, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can, and he says these pesukim cannot be understood at the surface level.

title.en: Chapter 11: the rasha v'tov lo

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the levels learned so far and begins chapter 11 on the rasha v'tov lo: at the moment he sins his good is subordinate to the kelipah in the left chamber of the heart, yet he is no complete rasha, since his yetzer tov remains strong. This too divides into countless levels, the lightest being one whose evil overcomes him only rarely and briefly in a small matter.

title.en: Why a thought of sin is worse than a sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why thoughts of sin can in a sense be worse than the sin itself: thought reaches far higher than speech and action, so it brings impurity into a higher sphere. He illustrates with a grease spot that is nothing on the street but disgraceful in the king's palace, mentions wasting free time that could be used for Torah, and explains that at the moment of such a lapse the person is a rasha v'tov lo until his good prevails.

title.en: Many levels of the rasha v'tov lo

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a lower rasha v'tov lo who sins several times a day, like one who learns, davens and gives tzedakah but habitually speaks lashon hara, and brings Chazal that reshaim are full of regret. He stresses that no one is sold to the yetzer hara beyond return, and closes that every person has a deep chamber in the heart that is a tzaddik gamur, which truly means 'l'shem yichud'.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the nine days, the Mashgiach explains that the bris removes the orlah that covers kedusha, in a person, in a place and in time, and that the mourning set aside for a bris in these days is a sign that Hashem will remove the orlah of churban and reveal their greatness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks what connection a bris has to the customs of the nine days, which are set aside for it: the participants may eat meat, drink wine and take a haircut. He explains that a bris removes the orlah from the holy covenant and reveals the kedusha of the Jewish child, and that, following Sefer Yetzirah, there is orlah in a person, in a place and in time. Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, the place of the Mikdash and the Shechinah, are now covered by an orlah made by the galus, which Moshiach will remove. These days too, which the holy sefarim call great days and which Zechariah says will turn to joy, are covered by the orlah of churban. A bris in the nine days, when the mourning is lifted, is therefore a sign that the orlah of the time will be removed, and he blesses that Eliyahu HaNavi come and bring the geulah.

en: The bris sets aside the mourning customs of the nine days: meat, wine and haircuts are permitted to those taking part.
A bris removes the orlah and reveals the kedusha that is covered in a Jewish child.
Orlah exists in three dimensions, in a person, in a place and in time.
Eretz Yisrael, the place of the Mikdash, is now covered by an orlah made by the galus, which Moshiach will remove to reveal the Shechinah.
The days of the three weeks are destined to be great days, but are now covered by the orlah of churban.

candidateTopics: orlah in person, place and time
bein hametzarim as days of future joy

title.en: Orlah over a child and over the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a bris sets aside the customs of the nine days, and explains that a bris removes the orlah from a child's kedusha. Orlah exists in a person, a place and time; Eretz Yisrael, the place of the Mikdash, is now covered by the orlah of galus.

title.en: The orlah of the time and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that these days are destined to be great days, as Zechariah says, but are covered by the orlah of churban; a bris now, when the mourning is lifted, is a sign that Hashem will remove that orlah. He closes with blessings that Eliyahu HaNavi come and bring the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris seudah, the Mashgiach explains that while every generation, year and moment has its own task, the bris is the eternal covenant that carries Yiddishkeit and emunah unchanged from one generation to the next.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'to pass into the covenant' from Parshas Nitzavim and explains that a bris is something made eternal. He brings Rashi in Parshas Noach that a covenant was needed so the fruits would not spoil. Every generation, year and moment has its own conduct and task, to be fulfilled in its time, yet beneath the change runs the eternity of Klal Yisroel: to be Hashem's chosen people, do His will and crown Him King over the world. Names change with each mission, as Rashi says, but this never changes. Milah, unlike other mitzvos, hands emunah from one generation to the next, a covenant made even with the unborn. Amalek, who scorned milah, fights this eternity, so Hashem's war with him lasts from generation to generation. The Mashgiach closes with blessings.

en: A bris is something made eternal: like the covenant over the fruits in Noach's ark, it is what keeps a thing from spoiling.
Every generation, year and moment has its own conduct and its own task that must be fulfilled at that time.
Beneath every change there is an eternity of Klal Yisroel that never changes, and this is the meaning of the bris.
The Jewish people's task, to be Hashem's chosen people, do His will and crown Him King over the whole world, does not change from day to day, year to year or generation to generation.
Milah differs from other mitzvos: it is the handing down of emunah and Yiddishkeit from one generation to the next.
Amalek, who scorned milah, is the force that opposes the eternity of Klal Yisroel, and so Hashem's war with him is from generation to generation.

title.en: The bris as what makes things eternal

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'to pass into the covenant' from Parshas Nitzavim and Rashi in Parshas Noach on the covenant over the fruits, and explains that a bris preserves. He contrasts this with the changing conduct of every generation, year and moment, beneath which runs the eternity of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Milah: handing emunah to the next generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Jewish people's role toward Hashem never changes, though names change with each mission, and that milah, unlike other mitzvos, carries emunah from generation to generation, a covenant made even with the unborn. He then explains Amalek, who scorned milah, as the force opposing this eternity, hence the war 'from generation to generation'.

title.en: The father's mesirus nefesh and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the father's mesirus nefesh for emunah and Yiddishkeit, says this gives an assurance that Amalek will have no hold here, and that today's bris is made with the generations to come. He closes with blessings that Yiddishkeit continue in the family and that Hashem's kingship be revealed over the whole world.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach explains why the Harachaman for Moshiach mentions the 'chasan damim' of Moshe Rabbeinu's son, and why a bris in a time of weakened milah is a harbinger of the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Harachaman prayers said at a bris and asks why the one for Moshiach is tied to the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos', the milah of Moshe Rabbeinu's son, and why it speaks of good tidings. He asks how Moshe Rabbeinu could have delayed his son's milah, and compares it to the Midrash on the breaking of the luchos: Moshe did not want to be separated from klal Yisroel. Using the Ibn Ezra that milah is a sign by which Jews recognize one another, he explains that the punishment of kareis for not doing milah, like that for eating on Yom Kippur, comes from cutting oneself off from the community. In Egypt the Jews had stopped doing milah, and Moshe, pained by this, held back his own son's milah to arouse mercy above for all of them. Today too milah has been weakened among millions of Jews, so a bris now is a sign that the geulah is near. He closes with blessings for the family.

en: The Mashgiach asks why the Harachaman for Moshiach is said in the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos', when Moshiach should come in his own merit.
Following the Ibn Ezra, the Mashgiach says milah is a sign by which Jews everywhere recognize one another as Jews.
The kareis for not doing milah, like the kareis for eating on Yom Kippur, is explained as the result of separating oneself from klal Yisroel.
Moshe Rabbeinu held back his son's milah because the Jews in Egypt were not circumcising, in order to arouse mercy above for them.
In our time, as before the Exodus, milah has been weakened among millions of Jews, so a bris now is a good sign that the geulah is coming.

candidateTopics: milah as a sign of Jewish identity
kareis and separation from the community

title.en: Harachaman, Moshiach and 'chasan damim'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Harachaman for Moshiach at a bris mentions the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos' and good tidings. He then asks how Moshe Rabbeinu could have delayed his son's milah, and points to the Midrash that Moshe broke the luchos because he did not want to be separate from klal Yisroel.

title.en: Milah as the sign of belonging to klal Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ibn Ezra that milah is a sign by which Jews recognize each other, and a sefer's explanation that kareis for eating on Yom Kippur comes from separating from the community; the same applies to milah. Since in Egypt the Jews had stopped doing milah, Moshe Rabbeinu held back his own son's milah to arouse mercy above, which is why it says 'lamulos' in the plural.

title.en: A bris today as a harbinger of the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares our time, before the geulah, to the time before the Exodus: milah has been weakened among millions of Jews in Russia, America and everywhere. Since Moshe Rabbeinu is connected to Moshiach, a bris in the week of the parsha of bris milah is a good sign of redemption; he ends with blessings for the father, the family and all present.

catalogTitle: רשע וטוב לו - יש לו חרטה אחר העבירות אבל לא עשה תשובה. רשע ורע לו - נשמות שמסר יעקב לעשו - אבל יש להם נקודת יחידה ומצטרפים למנין.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 11, the Mashgiach explains the rasha who still feels regret and the rasha in whom the good has departed, and shows that even the lowest Jew keeps a surrounding holiness that joins him to a minyan and that Purim, especially in Adar Sheni, celebrates.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 11. A rasha v'tov lo sins often, yet the living good in him brings thoughts of regret between his sins, though he lacks the strength to stop; the Slonimer Rebbe's mashal of the drunkard who rewarded his three sober days with a drink illustrates him. The rasha v'ra lo never thinks of teshuvah; these are the souls Yaakov sent to Esav, and the Midrash of the am ha'aretz shows they will return to Yaakov when Moshiach comes. The good in such a person has left its nest but hovers above him as a makif. In a long Purim digression the Mashgiach explains, through Amalek, the tribe of Dan, Haman's silver and the silver hooks of the Mishkan, that Hashem never rejects the Jews outside the camp. He then explains that this makif of Yechidah is why ten reshaim make a minyan, and closes with Adar Sheni, Shushan Purim in Yerushalayim, and questions from the listeners.

en: A rasha v'tov lo still has a living good inclination that brings regret between his sins, but it lacks the strength to make him abandon them.
A rasha v'ra lo never thinks of teshuvah; he is the counterpart of the tzaddik who never thinks of sinning.
The good that leaves such a person does not abandon him altogether but hovers above him as a makif, a surrounding light, like a bird hovering over its nest.

Above every Jew is a holiness of Yechidah, the fusion of all the souls of Klal Yisrael, that no sin can touch; it is revealed when ten Jews gather, which is why ten reshaim make a minyan and nine tzaddikim do not.
Hashem never rejects the Jews whom Amalek and Haman regarded as outcasts, and this is the special joy of Purim, especially in Adar Sheni.

candidateTopics: rasha v'tov lo and rasha v'ra lo
no Jew is rejected by Hashem

title.en: The rasha who still feels regret

summary.en: After finding the place in Tanya chapter 11, the Mashgiach explains that a momentary sinner is a rasha only at that moment, and then describes the rasha v'tov lo who sins often and harshly, yet has thoughts of teshuvah between his sins from the living good in him, without the strength to stop.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe's mashal of the drunkard

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Slonimer Rebbe's reading of the passuk 'mi yiten tahor mitamei lo echad' with the mashal of a drunkard who stayed sober three days and then rewarded himself with a drink, and applies it to the rasha who has regret but not the strength of a firm 'no'.

title.en: The souls Yaakov sent to Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that those ruled by the yetzer hara are the souls Yaakov sent to Esav, and tells the Midrash of an am ha'aretz who taught Rabbi Hoshaya that Esav's kings will return the gift to Moshiach; he explains that this was the am ha'aretz's own portion in the Torah, that these souls will return to Yaakov.

title.en: The rasha v'ra lo and the hovering good

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's description of the rasha v'ra lo, who never has thoughts of teshuvah because the good has left its place in his heart, and explains that it still hovers above him as a makif, like a bird above a nest occupied by a serpent, comparing it to the tzelem Elokim that hovers above a non-Jew.

title.en: Adar, the tribe of Dan and Amalek

summary.en: Turning to the month of Adar, the Mashgiach explains that Adar at the end of the year corresponds to the lowest souls, and recalls that the idol-carrying Jews of the camp of Dan were expelled from the Clouds of Glory and fell to Amalek; Hashem does not forgive Amalek for having no mercy on them, because no Jew is rejected by Him.

title.en: Haman's silver and the hooks of the Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman's ten thousand talents were meant to cancel the half-shekel of the six hundred thousand, but he did not redeem the surplus that became the silver hooks outside the holiness of the Mishkan, the portion of the rejected Jews; this was the 'parashas hakesef' Mordechai told Esther. He adds that the thirteenth month, Adar Sheni, lies outside the twelve combinations of Hashem's Name, and the Purim miracle happened in it.

title.en: Yechidah and the minyan of ten reshaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why ten reshaim make a minyan while nine tzaddikim cannot, and answers that above every Jew hovers a level of the soul, Kedushas Yisrael or Yechidah, the fusion of all souls in the soul of Yaakov Avinu, that no sin affects; Korach's flaw reached up to Levi but not to Yisrael, and ten Jews together reveal this makif.

title.en: The end of the perek and the Purim of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the last lines of the perek, that even the worst rasha has the makif above him and therefore Chazal say the Shechinah rests on every ten Jews, and returns to the joy of Adar Sheni; he explains that Purim is for the rasha who still has regret, and Shushan Purim of Yerushalayim, a walled city, is for those who have nothing but the makif.

title.en: Questions: the inner point, sukkah and the minyan

summary.en: Answering listeners, the Mashgiach explains that the point in every Jew is truly his, but it comes to expression only as a makif when he davens with a minyan; he compares the makif to the sukkah and says it can become inner on Simchas Torah. He adds that one guards against the contagion of rishus but must still care for the rasha, and that the minyan is learned from Korach's congregation.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach links the father's eight days of involvement in his son's milah to the Jew whose heart is always in Yerushalayim, and blesses him to merit seeing the Shechinah three times a year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Harachaman of the bris that links the milah on the eighth day to going up to see the Shechinah three times a year. He explains that a Jew longs all year for the time he can go to Yerushalayim for Yom Tov, and as the passuk says of the Beis HaMikdash, 'My eyes and My heart shall be there all the days': since his thoughts are there, it is as if he is there constantly. He then brings Tosafos' question why a passuk is needed to exempt a woman from milah, and an answer in the Rishonim: the father is bound by the mitzvah day and night for all eight days, since he must arrange that the bris be on time. Today, when problems with a bris on the eighth day are common and a father runs between doctor and rav, he is busy with the mitzvah all eight days; measure for measure, the Mashgiach blesses him to go up to Yerushalayim and see the Shechinah.

en: A Jew who longs all year for Yerushalayim has his heart there constantly, so it is as if he is always there.
According to an answer in the Rishonim, milah is not a time-bound mitzvah for the father, since he is obligated day and night for all eight days to make sure the bris happens on time.

When a father runs between doctor and rav for eight days and nights to arrange the bris, he is busy with the mitzvah the whole time, and measure for measure should merit going up to see the Shechinah.

title.en: Eight days of milah and the longing for Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the Harachaman's blessing to see the Shechinah three times a year with the eight days of milah. He explains that a Jew whose heart is always in Yerushalayim is as if there constantly, brings an answer in the Rishonim that the father is bound by the mitzvah all eight days, and applies it to a father who ran between doctor and rav to arrange the bris.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach explains that milah, Avraham Avinu's inheritance of emunah, is above daas, and that this bris joins that emunah with the daas of a family of Torah, like sasson (milah) together with yekar (tefillin).

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by tying milah specifically to Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, who left all Jewish children an inheritance of emunah. Emunah, he explains, is higher than daas, and the root of Klal Yisroel cannot be grasped by the mind. That is why milah is given to an eight-day-old infant who has no daas yet: one might ask why not wait until the child understands, but milah is entirely a matter of emunah above daas. He adds that even Jews who keep nothing else still keep milah, because a person can choose to be a tzaddik or a rasha but not whether to be a Jew. Turning to this bris, he cites Chazal that sasson is milah and yekar is tefillin: milah is wholly above daas, tefillin is the peak of daas, and this family, distinguished in Torah and yiras shamayim, joins the two. He ends with blessings for the child.

en: Milah is bound to Avraham Avinu, who left all Jewish children an inheritance of emunah.
Emunah is above daas, and the root of Klal Yisroel cannot be grasped by the mind.
Milah is given to an infant without daas, because it is entirely a matter of emunah above daas.
Even Jews who keep no other mitzvah keep milah, since being a Jew is beyond a person's free choice.
Sasson is milah, above daas; yekar is tefillin, the peak of daas; this bris joins the two.

title.en: Milah: Avraham's emunah above daas

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties milah to Avraham Avinu, the first believer, who left Jewish children an inheritance of emunah, which is above daas. He asks why milah is not delayed until the child has understanding, and answers that milah, like emunah, is above daas.

title.en: Sasson and yekar: milah with tefillin

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that even non-observant Jews keep milah, because being a Jew is beyond choice. He then brings Chazal that sasson is milah and yekar is tefillin, says this family of Torah joins emunah above daas with the peak of daas, and blesses the child.

catalogTitle: האדם נברא ביכולת שישליט המוח על הלב. יש לכל יהודי שורש הנעלם שכולו טוב. שייכות לפורים.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Mashgiach explains that the beinoni's evil is only subdued, not killed: it is silenced during true davening and wakes again afterward, yet his mind always has the power to rule over his heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 12 and explains that the beinoni, whose evil never overpowers the good, is what we would call a tzaddik, yet he keeps the potential to sin. Comparing it to the Rambam's testimony of the One Who knows hidden things about a baal teshuvah, he says the term describes a present, resolute condition. An antibiotics analogy shows the difference: the tzaddik killed his yetzer hara, the beinoni only knocked it out. He explains the three judges and why the beinoni still gets full credit. During davening, when a channel is cut upward through Pesukei Dezimra and the brachos of Krias Shema, the beinoni rises like a tzaddik; afterward he falls back, like a dancer landing. Finally, an undesirable thought is no failing but a chance for the mitzvah of not straying after the heart, since the mind was created to rule the heart.

en: The beinoni of Tanya never sins and would seem a tzaddik to us, but his yetzer hara is still alive within him.
Being a beinoni describes a present resolute state, so a later sin does not mean he never was one, and teshuvah restores it.
The tzaddik has killed his yetzer hara, while the beinoni has only knocked it out, so it may revive.
During true davening the beinoni's evil is rendered powerless and he is like a tzaddik, but after davening it awakens again.
Pesukei Dezimra cut a channel up through the obstructions, and the brachos of Krias Shema bring down yiras Shamayim and ahavah.
An undesirable thought is not a failing but a chance for the mitzvah of not straying after one's heart; the sin is only letting it linger.
Every person was created with a mind that can rule his heart, so there is no excuse to say he cannot control his thoughts.

title.en: Who is the beinoni of chapter 12

summary.en: After greeting a new listener, the Mashgiach opens chapter 12 on the beinoni, whose evil never overpowers the good, and explains that we would call him a tzaddik. The real tzaddik, like Dovid HaMelech, has killed the yetzer hara in the left chamber of his heart and replaced it with good.

title.en: A present state, like the Rambam's teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beinoni's yetzer hara is suppressed but still there, and that being a beinoni describes his present resolute condition, as the Rambam says of a baal teshuvah that the One Who knows hidden things testifies about him. An analogy of antibiotics taken for too short a time shows the difference between knocking out the yetzer hara and killing it.

title.en: Rasha, tzaddik v'ra lo and the three judges

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Mashgiach distinguishes the rasha and the tzaddik v'ra lo from the beinoni, then explains the judges: the yetzer hara judges the rasha, the yetzer tov the tzaddik, and both the beinoni. Hashem helps the beinoni, and with the passuk 'Hashem lo ya'azvenu' he explains that at the judgment he still gets full credit.

title.en: No barrier: the beinoni's davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sins create a barrier between a person and his neshamah, so his thoughts wander in davening; he brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word of tefillah is a heichal from which the unworthy are thrown out. The beinoni has no such barrier, so while davening he feels the malachim singing and has the status of a tzaddik.

title.en: A person is where his thought is

summary.en: On the Tanya's 'special times' of davening, the Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, proves it from the halachah of designating a tree as one's Shabbos resting place, which he saw in the Satmar Rav and the Avnei Nezer, and applies it to having Yerushalayim in mind in davening.

title.en: The eis ratzon that moves with the sunrise

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how an eis ratzon outside Eretz Yisrael can be real when everything follows Eretz Yisrael, noting that the Ramak says those abroad miss out and the Ba'al HaTanya in his Shulchan Aruch disagrees. He explains that Above there is no time, and the eis ratzon formed at sunrise moves along with the sunrise, which is why Shacharis is the main time and needs a long davening with tallis and tefillin.

title.en: Cutting a channel: the order of davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the air up to Shamayim is full of klipos from people's sins, and Pesukei Dezimra cut a channel through them, as the Arizal reads 'zimra' as cutting. Then the brachos of Krias Shema bring down yiras Shamayim and ahavah, preparing for Shema itself, and the bracha after Shema extends yetzias Mitzrayim, freeing oneself from everything that keeps him from Hashem.

title.en: Rising in davening, falling back after

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that during genuine davening the beinoni's evil becomes subservient to the good and powerless, since even the body sees its root, as the chayos rise to the level of the serafim. After davening the motor shuts off and he falls back, like Chassidim who dance and rise off the ground only for a moment; the evil wakes again but remains only one judge.

title.en: Undesirable thoughts and 'machshavah mamash'

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that an undesirable thought comes from the yetzer hara, not from the person's essence, and is no reason to feel guilty; it is an opportunity for the mitzvah of 'v'lo sasuru', which is transgressed only by letting the thought linger. He explains that the beinoni never lets in a 'machshavah mamash', a fully developed thought.

title.en: The mind rules the heart; Reb Shmelke's dveikus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mind is the ruler over the heart and every person was created able to hold himself back. He tells of the Rebbe Reb Shmelke, who asked his students to tap him if he lost his dveikus while learning, and explains that Torah learned with dveikus is like tefillah, but the Tanya speaks of tefillah. He ends answering a question about Pesukei Dezimra and the eis ratzon.

oneLiner.en: At a bris held minutes before sunset in the week of parshas Shemos, the Mashgiach explains that milah is bound up with the geulah, and that a bris that cannot be pushed off any later should arouse Heaven that the geulah cannot wait.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Chazal that Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised and asks: milah exists to cut away the bad, and the Chinuch says man was created incomplete so that he should perfect himself, so why was Moshe born already circumcised? He answers that milah, the eighth, belongs to the days of Moshiach, and Moshe is the first and final redeemer. Following the Maharal, a redeemer must stand outside what he redeems, so Moshe, who will remove idolatry from the world, had to be a 'mohel' from birth, and Dovid too was born circumcised as the soul of Moshiach. He then brings Avraham Avinu's zerizus and the custom to do a bris early in the morning, since milah is a plea for the geulah to come quickly. This bris, delayed until minutes before sunset, he reads as a sign that the geulah cannot wait, and he blesses the child, named after two tzaddikim.

en: Moshe Rabbeinu was born circumcised, which seems to contradict the purpose of milah as a person's own perfection.
Milah, the eighth, is connected to the days of Moshiach, and Moshe is both the first and the final redeemer.
A redeemer must be outside what he redeems, so Moshe and Dovid, the redeemers, were born circumcised.
A bris is done early in the morning out of zerizus, following Avraham Avinu, because milah is a plea for a speedy geulah.
A bris pushed to the last minutes before sunset signals that the geulah too can no longer be delayed.

title.en: Why Moshe was born circumcised

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Moshe was born circumcised when milah is meant for a person to perfect himself. He answers that milah belongs to Moshiach, that Moshe is the first and final redeemer, and that, per the Maharal, a redeemer must stand outside the impurity he removes, as Dovid too was born circumcised.

title.en: A bris at sunset: the geulah cannot wait

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Avraham Avinu's zerizus and the custom of an early-morning bris as a plea for a quick geulah. He then reads this bris, held minutes before sunset in the week of parshas Shemos, as a sign that the geulah cannot be delayed, and blesses the child named after two tzaddikim.

oneLiner.en: At the bris of a boy named Dovid, the Mashgiach explains Chazal that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised: born of a refined lineage, he had no waste to remove, and the name Dovid points to purity and temimus.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach notes that the child is named Dovid after a relative who was no ordinary Jew, a man of mesirus nefesh and Yiddishkeit, as his children and grandchildren show. He brings the Gemara that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised, reading 'michtam l'Dovid' as 'his wound was whole'. A child, he says, has a connection to the first bearer of his name, as a child named Avraham connects to Avraham's yiras shamayim. Milah normally cuts away the waste in a child, but Dovid, descended from Yehudah, Peretz, Nachshon, Boaz and Yishai, was born refined, with no waste needing removal. A child named Dovid, from a family of Torah, yiras shamayim and chessed on all sides, carries that purity and temimus, and the Mashgiach blesses him to grow to Torah, chuppah and good deeds.

en: The child is named Dovid after a relative of mesirus nefesh and Yiddishkeit, visible in his descendants.
Chazal teach from 'michtam l'Dovid' that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised.
A child bearing a name has a connection to the first bearer of that name.
Milah cuts away the waste in a child, but Dovid, from a refined lineage, had none to remove.

title.en: The name Dovid and a pure bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the relative the child Dovid is named after, brings Chazal that Dovid HaMelech was born circumcised, and explains that his refined lineage left no waste for milah to remove. He ties the name Dovid to purity and temimus and blesses the child.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach ties milah to Yom Kippur and the days of Sefirah, and explains that the father who brings his son into the covenant draws upon himself the soul of Avraham Avinu, and that the name is given at the milah because milah leaves a lasting remembrance.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the weeks of Acharei and Kedoshim and says that Yom Kippur is, in its essence, the matter of milah: the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer says Avraham's bris was on Yom Kippur, and the passuk 'Hashem will circumcise your heart' joins the two. He connects a Masorah mnemonic for the Yom Kippur parsha to the sefirah of yesod, which is milah, as the Zohar says. He then tells what Rabbi Chaim Vital wrote: the Arizal stood up for him because, while busy with redeeming captives, he carried the soul of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair. So too a father who brings his child into the bris of Avraham receives Avraham's soul that day, the trait of chessed. He notes the auspicious time and the child's name, Yaakov Yosef, and blesses the family. In a second part he explains, from Amalek's scorn for milah and his punishment of having his remembrance erased, why the name is given at the milah.

en: The Mashgiach says Yom Kippur is in essence the matter of milah, since Avraham Avinu's bris was on Yom Kippur.
He links the sefirah of yesod to the mitzvah of milah and finds a hint to milah in the Masorah of the Yom Kippur parsha.
A person busy with a mitzvah that a tzaddik was connected to receives that tzaddik's soul; so a father bringing his son into the bris receives the soul of Avraham Avinu that day.
Amalek scorned milah and was punished measure for measure by having his remembrance erased; milah, by contrast, leaves a remembrance, which is why the name is given at the milah.

naming a child at the bris

title.en: Yom Kippur as the matter of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that Yom Kippur, read in Parshas Acharei, is in essence the matter of milah, citing the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that Avraham's bris was on Yom Kippur and the passuk of circumcising the heart. He ties a Masorah mnemonic for that parsha to the sefirah of yesod, which is milah.

title.en: Receiving Avraham Avinu's soul at the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Arizal stood up for Rabbi Chaim Vital because, busy with redeeming captives, he carried the soul of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, and applies it: a father bringing his son into the bris receives the soul of Avraham Avinu. He speaks of the auspicious time of Sefirah and the name Yaakov Yosef, and blesses the family.

title.en: Why the name is given at the milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings that Amalek scorned milah and was punished measure for measure with the erasing of his remembrance, and explains that milah leaves a lasting remembrance, which is why the child's name is given at the milah. He closes with a blessing for the child.

catalogTitle: ביאור איך הבינוני מנצח נסיונות בין אדם לחבירו. אהבת ה' ואהבת ישראל אחד. פורים וי"ג יו"ט של לך כנוס וכו'.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Mashgiach explains that the Beinoni's mind rules his heart while his hidden love for Hashem lies dormant, shows through the 'tip of the yud' how this innermost point is revealed on Yom Kippur and even more on Purim, and ends with how the Beinoni overcomes ill will toward his fellow Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews that in the Beinoni the evil inclination is knocked out but still speaks, and that the mind rules the heart by nature, so even Haman could restrain himself. Since light pushes away darkness, bad thoughts are best displaced with holiness. The Beinoni is still not a tzaddik: his advantage is only in function, while in his core lies a hidden love. Through the Gemara on the Purim decree, the forty lashes reduced to thirty-nine, the Rambam on a forced get and the 'tip of the yud', the Mashgiach shows that sin never reaches the fortieth level, revealed on Yom Kippur, on Purim, and through Mordechai's self-sacrifice. He returns to the Beinoni, whose love sleeps after davening, explains why Tanya omits avak lashon hara, how the Beinoni repels thoughts, and how he answers hostility toward a fellow Jew with kindness, closing with a Chassidic story.

en: In the Beinoni the evil inclination still voices its opinion but is never listened to, because by nature the mind rules over the heart.
The Beinoni's advantage is only in his functioning, his thought, speech and action, not in his essence, which is why he is not called a tzaddik.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem in the depths of his heart, a fortieth level, the 'tip of the yud', that sin never reaches.
The atonement of Yom Kippur, and even more the salvation of Purim, come from this innermost place, opened by self-sacrifice.
A passing thought of sin is not a sin for the Beinoni; pushing it away immediately is a mitzvah.
Between man and his fellow, the Beinoni dismisses any feeling of hostility and does the very opposite, treating the other kindly.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, even in Haman

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that the Beinoni's evil inclination is knocked out but still speaks, reads that the mind rules the heart by nature, and shows it from Haman restraining himself before Mordechai. Bad thoughts are best displaced with holiness.

title.en: Light over darkness; why only a Beinoni

summary.en: With the candle that drives darkness from a whole room, the Mashgiach explains how holiness pushes away the folly of sin. He then asks why so perfect a person is only called a Beinoni, and answers that his advantage is only in function, not essence, like a dancer who must come down.

title.en: The hidden love and the Purim decree

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the Beinoni's heart lies a hidden, natural love of the G-dly soul. He brings the Gemara where Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says the Jews bowed only outwardly, asks how he knew this, and answers that every Jew has a hidden chamber that protests against sin.

title.en: Forty levels and the tip of the yud

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that creation and man consist of forty forces, the fortieth being the 'tip of the yud' of Hashem's Name, where no sin reaches. With the Rambam on a get given under duress, he shows that the inner will remains good, so lashes are only thirty-nine.

title.en: Yom Kippur, Amalek and Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ba'al HaTanya on 'before Hashem you shall be purified': Yom Kippur atones from the Holy of Holies, above the yud. Amalek is the 'first' of impurity set against it. Purim, he says, is even higher than Yom Kippur, and its intoxication is like anesthesia for those who reach it.

title.en: Esther's fear and Mordechai ben Kish

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Esther's fear that the Jews had sinned even against the innermost point, which Amalek sought to occupy. Hashem Himself judged by the inner point, and Mordechai, 'ben Kish' who knocked on the gates of mercy, sparked the self-sacrifice that opened them.

title.en: Self-sacrifice opens the hidden chamber

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the gates of the Holy of Holies open on Yom Kippur through the fast, which is self-sacrifice, and on Purim through the Jews' self-sacrifice. This hidden love is why even sinners gave their lives rather than worship idols, and why the Jews did not abandon their Jewishness to escape Haman's decree.

title.en: The tzaddik's open love, the Beinoni's dormant love

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the tzaddik, who is himself a Holy of Holies like Aharon, with the Beinoni, whose love glows openly only while davening and lies dormant afterward. He may still feel worldly desires, but never acts on them.

title.en: Thoughts of sin and avak lashon hara

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why thoughts of sin are worse than the sin, that a passing thought is no sin for the Beinoni who repels it, and why the Tanya mentions only two of the three sins no one escapes daily, leaving out avak lashon hara.

title.en: The imprint of davening repels thoughts

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that being a Beinoni is a great level, that the imprint of davening and the hidden fear and love help him rule over the heart, and that he pushes a bad thought away with both hands. Impurity rises from heart to mind, but without lingering it bears nothing and dissipates.

title.en: Between man and his fellow: doing the opposite

summary.en: Reading the Tanya on matters between man and his fellow, the Mashgiach explains that the Beinoni dismisses hostility and does the opposite, as Yosef did with his brothers. He tells of the Lechovitcher Rebbe and a Chassid whose competitor opened a store across the street, and answers a listener's objection.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Mashgiach contrasts Esav's meal that despised the birthright with the pidyon haben meal that honors the firstborn, Hashem who is First, and the Torah called 'reishis', and explains why eating at it is likened to eighty-four fasts.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach says pidyon haben comes from the Exodus, when Hashem said 'sanctify to Me every firstborn', and that on the night of the plague of the firstborn Jews reached a conduct above intellect and time, tied to 'Bereishis', the first utterance. He relates a sefer's account of a Nittel night and says that at a pidyon haben meal such forces have no hold. From 'My firstborn son is Israel' he turns to Esav's meal, where he despised the birthright, and asks why that is stressed when Esav did worse that day. Using Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's reading of the Rambam on techiyas hameisim, he answers that despising the birthright revealed denial of 'reishis'. The pidyon haben meal is the reverse: it honors the firstborn and the Torah. He explains the saying that such a meal equals eighty-four fasts, notes how Maseches Pesachim ends, and blesses the family.

en: Pidyon haben comes from the Exodus, when on the night of the plague of the firstborn Jews reached a conduct above intellect and above time.
Relative to the angels, the Mashgiach says, Jews are Hashem's firstborn; the verse does not mean that the nations are ordinary sons.
Esav's despising the birthright was singled out because it revealed that he denied 'reishis', the firstness through which Israel and the Torah are bound to Hashem.
The pidyon haben meal is the reverse of Esav's meal: it honors the birthright and the Torah and gives thanks to Hashem.
Eating at a pidyon haben meal is likened to eighty-four fasts, because honoring 'reishis' repairs the root blemish of the first not being given to Hashem.

title.en: Pidyon haben and the night of the Exodus

summary.en: Asked by the father to speak, the Mashgiach says pidyon haben stems from 'sanctify to Me every firstborn' at the Exodus, when Jews reached a conduct above intellect and time. He relates a sefer's account of a Nittel night and says that at a pidyon haben meal such forces have no hold, as on the night when 'no dog sharpened its tongue'.

title.en: Esav's meal and the pidyon haben meal

summary.en: From 'My firstborn son is Israel' the Mashgiach turns to Esav's meal at which he despised the birthright, and asks why this is stressed when Esav did worse that day. Through Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's reading of the Rambam on techiyas hameisim he answers that it revealed denial of 'reishis', and calls the pidyon haben meal its reverse, a meal honoring the birthright and the Torah.

title.en: A meal equal to eighty-four fasts

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings from the seforim that eating at a pidyon haben meal is like the eighty-four fasts the Arizal gave for a blemish of the bris, and explains that the root blemish is the first not going to Hashem, so honoring 'reishis' repairs it. He notes that Maseches Pesachim ends with the father's blessing, and blesses the family and all of Israel with redemption.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Mashgiach explains with a Chasam Sofer on Haman that the holiness of Israel is 'reishis', a holiness of the body that cannot be exchanged, and that the pidyon haben reveals this and arouses the redemption of Hashem's firstborn.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach repeats a Chasam Sofer on Haman's words 'there is one people scattered among the nations': Haman thought Israel's holiness was a holiness of value, which can be redeemed or exchanged, and that scattered among seventy nations it would be nullified. But Israel is 'reishis', with a holiness of the body. This holiness of reishis is the whole matter of the Exodus, when Israel was called Hashem's firstborn and the mitzvah of sanctifying and redeeming the firstborn was given. Hashem may place Israel's suffering on the nations, but Israel itself cannot be exchanged, as Bilaam wished. The Mashgiach explains Rashi's sharpness against one who says terumah can be redeemed. He then says the firstborn is the reishis from which the blessing of the later children flows, and that the pidyon haben arouses Hashem's redemption of Israel, and closes with a prayer for the final redemption.

en: Following the Chasam Sofer, Haman thought Israel had only a holiness of value, which can be exchanged or nullified among the nations.
Israel is 'reishis', with a holiness of the body that cannot be exchanged, and this is the whole matter of the Exodus.
Hashem can transfer what is decreed on Israel onto the nations, but Israel itself cannot be exchanged for another nation.
The firstborn is the reishis from which the blessing of the later children comes, and the pidyon haben reveals Israel's holiness of reishis and arouses the redemption.

title.en: Haman and the holiness of reishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach repeats the Chasam Sofer that Haman thought Israel's holiness could be exchanged or nullified among seventy nations, but Israel is 'reishis', with a holiness of the body. This holiness is the matter of the Exodus and of the firstborn, and while Israel's suffering can be transferred to the nations, Israel itself cannot be exchanged, as Bilaam wished.

title.en: Redeeming terumah, the firstborn and the redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Rashi is so sharp against one who says terumah can be redeemed, and answers that Israel is 'reishis', and those who hold that reishis can be redeemed are Bilaam and his students. He explains that the firstborn is the reishis from which later children's blessing comes, and that the pidyon haben arouses Hashem's redemption of Israel, closing with a prayer for the final redemption.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Mashgiach explains that holiness hidden in parents is revealed in their children, and that both havdalah and pidyon haben protect a place from which holiness has departed.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara on how many havdalos one says, where Rabbi Menachem bar Simai, called 'the son of holy ones', says only one. He was called this because he never looked at the image on a coin, and the Yerushalmi says he never did so at all, so he was born that way and drew the holiness from his parents. The Mashgiach explains with the Ramban on 'a root bearing gall and wormwood' that what is hidden in parents comes out openly in the children: his parents never thought about money, so their son would not even look at it. He then brings the Or HaChaim on why tumas ohel applies to Jews: where great holiness departed, the impure forces gather. Every motza'ei Shabbos the extra soul leaves, so people make three havdalos for protection, while Rabbi Menachem needed only one to fulfil the mitzvah. Finally he links pidyon haben to 'pedus' as separation, and blesses the family.

en: Rabbi Menachem bar Simai never looked at the image on a coin, and since he never did so even as a child, his holiness came from his parents.
What is hidden and inward in the parents becomes openly revealed in the children.
A place from which great holiness has departed draws the forces of impurity, which is why tumas ohel applies to Jews.
Havdalah protects the place left empty when the extra soul of Shabbos departs; ordinary people say three havdalos, while Rabbi Menachem needed only one.
Pidyon haben is connected to 'pedus', which the commentators read as a separation, like havdalah, between Jews and the nations.

candidateTopics: separation of Israel from the nations

title.en: The 'son of holy ones' and inherited holiness

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara about Rabbi Menachem bar Simai, who never looked at the image on a coin, and asks why he is called 'son of holy ones'. Using the Ramban on 'a root bearing gall and wormwood', he explains that what is hidden in parents is revealed in their children.

title.en: Havdalah and the empty place left by Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains havdalah as protection against the forces of impurity when the extra soul of Shabbos departs, bringing the Or HaChaim on tumas ohel. Ordinary people make three havdalos, but Rabbi Menachem bar Simai needed only one, to fulfil the mitzvah.

title.en: Pidyon haben as a separation, and a brachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects 'pedus' in the passuk to a separation between Jews and the nations, and explains that the firstborn must be redeemed because the holiness meant for him has departed. He closes by blessing the child that the holiness of his parents be revealed in him.

catalogTitle: הקב"ה עוזר לבינוני - “כי יעמוד לימין אביון.” י"ג ביאור מאמר חז"ל "אפ' כל העולם וכו' היה בעיניך כרשע." בינוני כצדיק בעיתות רצון. ביאור ענין עתות רצון.

oneLiner.en: Starting from the beinoni who uproots every grudge against a fellow Jew, the Mashgiach shows how the unity of Klal Yisrael reaches the level of keser on Yom Kippur and Purim, and then begins Tanya chapter thirteen: Hashem is the third judge who helps the beinoni.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach finishes the Tanya's description of the beinoni, who rejects every grudge against another Jew and neutralizes anger with compassion, repaying bad with good as Yosef did with his brothers. He then asks how love for every Jew fits with loving Hashem with the whole heart, and answers that a Jew is a part of G-d and all souls are one. That collective soul, beyond the reach of sin, is keser: Moshe Rabbeinu, the half-shekel, the goral of Yom Kippur and of Purim. Haman drew on the keser of impurity, and Esther's counsel to gather all the Jews answered him with unity, which Purim renews through shared food. After explaining why Yosef tested his brothers, the Mashgiach opens chapter thirteen: in the beinoni both inclinations are judges, and Hashem, the third judge, decides for the good.

en: The beinoni lets no grudge against another Jew settle in his mind; he rejects it and neutralizes it with love of Israel and compassion.
Love for every Jew does not divide the love of Hashem, because a Jew's soul is a part of G-d and all Jewish souls are one.
There is a level, called keser, where all souls fuse into one and no sin reaches; Yom Kippur and Purim, both decided by a goral, come from there.
Haman drew on the keser of impurity, and Esther answered him with unity, gathering all the Jews, which reaches the top of keser in holiness.
In the beinoni both the good and the evil inclination are judges voicing opinions, and Hashem is the third judge who tips the scale toward the good.

candidateTopics: Hashem helps against the yetzer hara

title.en: The beinoni uproots grudges

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues the Tanya's account of the beinoni, who rejects any hatred or grudge against a Jew as soon as it surfaces. He explains that compassion neutralizes anger, and that one should repay those who wronged him with good.

title.en: Yosef's test with his brothers

summary.en: The Zohar learns this from Yosef and his brothers. The Mashgiach cites his father-in-law's explanation that the brothers' enmity was sent from Heaven so that Yosef would be tested whether he would bear a grudge, and that he passed it in their merit.

title.en: Can love be divided?

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the question that love cannot be divided, so how can one love Hashem with all one's heart and also love every Jew. He answers that a Jew is a part of G-d and all Jews are one soul, and brings a sefer that ties the half-shekel to the skull.

title.en: The collective soul and Moshe Rabbeinu

summary.en: Citing the Noam Elimelech, the Mashgiach describes a height where all souls fuse into one, called Yisrael, which no sin can reach. Moshe Rabbeinu is that collective soul, and the half-shekel and the sockets made from it represent every Jew.

title.en: The goral of Yom Kippur and keser

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah that the two goats of Yom Kippur must be equal, and Rav Tzadok's explanation: at times Yaakov and Esav cannot be told apart, and only Hashem knows the hidden root where every Jew is a tzaddik. That level is keser, revealed on Yom Kippur and Purim through a goral.

title.en: Haman, Mordechai and the keser of impurity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Parshandasa is the keser of the klipah and that Haman sought to fight Mordechai's keser of holiness, even preventing him from saying Shema. When Haman rose higher in impurity, Esther's counsel to gather all the Jews answered him with unity, and so he is called the 'binder' of the Jews.

title.en: Purim unity through food

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the unity in Shushan alone with that of all the Jews on Purim. Using the eiruv, where shared food makes people one household, he explains that mishloach manos joins all of Klal Yisrael, just as a grudge spoils Yom Kippur.

title.en: Why Yosef tested his brothers

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach links Yosef to the power of unity and to the month of Adar. He then explains that Yosef pressed his brothers so their suffering would complete the repair of his sale, and that he could not hold back the few more moments needed.

title.en: Hashem, the third judge

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter thirteen, the Mashgiach explains Chazal's saying that in the beinoni both inclinations judge: each voices an opinion, and Hashem, who stands at the right of the needy, is the deciding judge. He brings the Maggid Meisharim on the verse 'Hashem will not leave him in his hand'.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seudah of a pidyon haben, unlike Esav's feast over despising the bechorah, honors the Jewish people's status as Hashem's firstborn, His 'reishis', and that even the last generations share in that status.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the custom of performing the pidyon haben in the middle of the seudah for publicity, and asks why this mitzvah needs more publicity than others. He turns to the parsha of the festivals, where the Torah interrupts the omer and Shavuos with the mitzvos of leket and peah. He then explains that Esav's sin in despising the bechorah was a flaw in his outlook, since the bechorah stands for the chosenness of Israel, the 'reishis' for whose sake the world was created. Esav even made a feast over it; the seudah of pidyon haben does the opposite and shows honor for the bechorah, which is greater than the mitzvah itself. The theme of reishis runs from Pesach to Shavuos. The forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field stand for the last generations, which are as precious as the first fruits, and the seudah is a chizuk in these times.

en: The custom is to perform the pidyon haben in the middle of the seudah, as a matter of publicizing the mitzvah.
The bechorah stands for the chosenness of Israel, called 'reishis', for whose sake the whole world was created.
Esav's despising of the bechorah was a sin of outlook, not of desire or anger, and only an Esav can stumble in it.
The seudah of pidyon haben is the reverse of Esav's feast: Jews make a seudah to honor the bechorah.
Honoring the bechorah is greater than the mitzvah of the bechorah itself, as honor of the Torah is greater than its study.
The last generations, like the forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field, are as precious to Hashem as the first fruits.

title.en: Why the pidyon haben is done mid-seudah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that, unlike other mitzvos, the pidyon haben is performed in the middle of the seudah for publicity, and asks why. He turns to the parsha of the festivals, the omer and the count to Shavuos, and to Rashi's question why leket and peah interrupt the festivals.

title.en: Esav despised the bechorah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah stresses that Esav despised the bechorah while not mentioning the five grave sins he did that day. He explains that the bechorah is the chosenness of Israel, the 'reishis' for which the world was created, and that the bechorah belongs to whoever wants to serve Hashem.

title.en: A sin of outlook, and Esav's feast

summary.en: Through Rav Tzadok's reading of the Chazal on techiyas hameisim, the Mashgiach explains that despising the bechorah is a symptom of having no share in it, a sin only an Esav commits. Esav even made a feast over it, and the seudah of pidyon haben expresses the opposite: a Jew's joy in his share in Israel's 'reishis'.

title.en: Honor of the bechorah, and Esav's false reishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Megillah that honor of the Torah outweighs its study, and says the seudah, honoring the bechorah, is greater than the mitzvah itself. He shows that reishis runs through many mitzvos, and that Esav's and Amalek's 'reishis' is false, as shown by its lack of a good end.

title.en: From Pesach to Shavuos: the festival of reishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the time from Pesach to Shavuos as one long festival of reishis, in which a Jew identifies with Hashem's first 'produce' through the omer and the bikkurim. He then turns to the last generations, in a time of great hester panim, when it is hard to see that Jews are Hashem's reishis.

title.en: The last sheaves are also reishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that leket, shikchah and peah, the last grain of the field, stand for the last generations, which are as precious as the first fruits; this answers why they appear among the festivals. He concludes that a seudah of pidyon haben in these last generations is a great chizuk, and closes with a brachah for the true redemption.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Mashgiach explains that 'pedus', redemption, comes after the alphabetical order of the Tehillim is complete, showing that Hashem leads the Jewish people above the natural order, and that a pidyon haben is a segulah for salvation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that pidyon haben is a matter beyond explanation, and that its parsha comes from yetzias Mitzrayim and is written in the tefillin, shel rosh and shel yad. Bringing the Pri Tzaddik, he explains that creation runs on an order, the order of the aleph-beis. In the chapter of Tehillim 'I will bless Hashem at all times', the verses follow the aleph-beis to its end, and only then comes an added verse, 'Hashem redeems the soul of His servants'; the same happens in the chapter ending 'G-d, redeem Israel from all its troubles'. Redemption is thus a conduct above the order, Hashem's special way with the Jewish people. He adds that in the days of Shabbos Mevarchim Tamuz, times of strict judgment, a pidyon haben is a great segulah for the community and for those at the simcha, and closes with blessings for the family and for the complete redemption.

en: The parsha of pidyon haben comes from yetzias Mitzrayim and is part of the tefillin.
In Tehillim, the verse about redemption is added after the aleph-beis order is complete, showing that redemption is above the order.
Hashem conducts Himself with the Jewish people in a special way that is not bound by the order of creation.
In the days around Shabbos Mevarchim Tamuz, times of strict judgment, a pidyon haben is a great segulah for the community and for those who come to it.

title.en: Redemption beyond the aleph-beis order

summary.en: The Mashgiach says pidyon haben comes from yetzias Mitzrayim and is in the tefillin, then brings the Pri Tzaddik: in two alphabetical chapters of Tehillim, a verse of redemption is added after the aleph-beis ends, showing that redemption is above the order of creation.

title.en: A segulah in days of judgment, and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that redemption is Hashem's conduct above the order with the Jewish people, and that a pidyon haben around Shabbos Mevarchim Tamuz, a time of judgment, is a segulah for salvation for the community and for those present. He closes with blessings for the family and for the complete redemption.

oneLiner.en: Using the tradition that the ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, the Mashgiach reads the current century in Nitzavim-Vayelech: the hester panim of the Holocaust, the promise that the Torah will not be forgotten, and the geulah that is written before the galus.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that everything Moshe Rabbeinu foretold in Devarim about exile and return has come true, while the nations' scriptures avoid predictions, and the church now has a problem with Jews back in Eretz Yisroel and Jerusalem. He then brings a tradition in the name of the Vilna Gaon that the ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, the world's Erev Shabbos, with Nitzavim-Vayelech counted as one sedra and corresponding to the present century. He tells how, as a bochur on Rosh Hashanah of that century's first year, he learned that Hitler had invaded Poland. In Vayelech he reads the double hester panim, explained with a mashal of a child who does not even know his father is hiding, and the promise that the Torah will never be forgotten. Finally he asks why the geulah of Nitzavim precedes the galus of Vayelech, and answers from the Gemara that for Jews the cure comes before the blow. He closes urging the bochurim to prepare for Moshiach.

en: Everything Moshe Rabbeinu foretold about the Jewish people's exile and return has been fulfilled, while the nations' scriptures do not dare to predict the future.
The ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, and Nitzavim-Vayelech, counted as one sedra, corresponds to the present century.
The doubled hester panim in Vayelech means that even the hiding itself is hidden, which the Mashgiach calls the confused state of Jews after the Holocaust.
The promise that the Torah will not be forgotten from the mouths of Jewish children has held, while the cultures of the great nations have been forgotten.
For Jews Hashem prepares the cure before the blow, which is why the geulah of Nitzavim is written before the galus of Vayelech.
Moshiach is near, and the Mashgiach says one must prepare for him like for Shabbos: teshuvah, Torah and mitzvos, and good davening.

the torah will not be forgotten

title.en: Moshe's prophecies fulfilled before our eyes

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that everything Moshe Rabbeinu foretold in Devarim about exile and return has come true, while the nations' scriptures avoid predictions. He describes the church's problem with Jews, many of them Torah-observant, back in Eretz Yisroel and the Old City of Jerusalem.

title.en: The ten sedras of Devarim and the ten centuries

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings in the name of the Vilna Gaon that the ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, the world's Erev Shabbos, with Nitzavim-Vayelech counted as one sedra. He tells of Rav Chaim of Volozhin asking the Gaon where he is hinted in Ki Seitzei, and concludes that the present century is found in Nitzavim-Vayelech.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah when Hitler entered Poland

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts how, as a bochur at the start of this century, he davened with his father on Rosh Hashanah and saw the congregation weeping because Hitler had invaded Poland. The war expected to last weeks lasted five years, and six million Jews were killed; the start of the century must therefore be found in Nitzavim-Vayelech.

title.en: Hester panim within hester panim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the pesukim in Vayelech where Hashem foretells that He will hide His face and many evils will befall the people, and asks what the doubled hiding means. With a mashal of a child chased by a tiger who does not even know his father is inside, he explains it as hiding within hiding, the state of Jews who lost their emunah in the Holocaust.

title.en: The song as witness; the Torah will not be forgotten

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem commands writing the song of Ha'azinu as a witness that He foretold the troubles, and promises the Torah will not be forgotten from the Jews' children. The cultures of Rome, Greece and Bavel are forgotten while Jews still learn Torah, even though Hitler specifically targeted the yeshivos and talmidei chachamim.

title.en: Why the geulah comes before the galus

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the promise of return and ingathering in Nitzavim and asks two questions: why this century is split over two sedras, and why the geulah in Nitzavim precedes the galus in Vayelech. He answers both from the Gemara that for Jews the cure comes before the blow, illustrated by Esther and Mordechai, a surgeon and a mohel, and explains that galus and geulah are two separate themes.

title.en: Preparing for Moshiach on the world's Erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bochurim that Moshiach is near, comparing the world to a barrel of gunpowder with a lit fuse. Like Erev Shabbos, one must do teshuvah, put on the Shabbos clothes of Torah and mitzvos, and daven well with a minyan, starting together word by word; he urges them to make a kiddush Hashem on their Shabbos away and closes with l'chaim.

catalogTitle: לבינוני אין לו כח לעקור הרע לגמרי אבל יכול י"ד לשלוט עליו בפועל ממש. ביאור איך העבירה הוא שטות. לבינוני יש תאוות לדברים גשמיים אבל מצד שורשו בקדושה הוא מואס ברע.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beinoni's mind can rule over his yetzer hara in deed but cannot uproot it, except in times of revealed love between Hashem and the Jew, such as davening and the month of Adar.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues the Tanya on the beinoni: he never sins, but the evil in the left chamber of the heart remains at full strength, and only Hashem's help lets him overcome it. This answers the Tanya's question from the first chapter: he is called 'like a rasha' because he could fall. He warns that the yetzer grows stronger with age and indulgence, and that constant learning is no sign it is gone. The mind rules the heart in thought, speech and deed, yet cannot expel the yetzer, except in times of revealed love, as in davening. From here he speaks of Hashem's hidden love for every Jew: the Ruzhiner's story, the father and son, the sin of the Golden Calf, and Purim, where the salvation was prepared at Achashverosh's party. He explains hester panim, the struggle of Yaakov and Esav, Yerushalayim and Rome, and Adar Sheni.

en: The beinoni never sins, but the yetzer hara in the left chamber of the heart remains as strong as at birth; he wins only because Hashem stands at his right side and helps him.
He is called 'like a rasha' because the potential to sin is fully alive in him, so he must not believe people who call him a tzaddik.
The mind was created with power to rule the heart's urges in thought, speech and deed, but not to uproot the yetzer itself.
In times of favor, above all during davening, the love of Hashem is revealed and the beinoni is temporarily like a tzaddik.
Hashem's love for every Jew is the unconditional love of a father for a child, concealed but revealed in times of favor, even through the people's sins.
Adar is a time of hester panim within which Hashem's hidden love is uncovered, as the Megillah shows the salvation being prepared during the sin itself.

Hashem's hidden love for every Jew
